answer_1.quote: Our ultimate goal is to develop a generation model p(u_t |u_{<t}) that can predict the next utterance based on the context of the conversation.

answer_2.quote: We choose three commonly used reference-based metrics including BLEU , METEOR (Lavie and Agarwal, 2007) and ROUGE , where BLEU and METEOR are computed with an open source NLG evaluation tool available at , and ROUGE is calculated with the code published at . We report the F1 scores for ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L. We also use Distinct to evaluate the lexical diversity with Distinct-1 and Distinct-2 denoting ratios of distinct unigrams and bigrams in responses, respectively.

answer_4.quote: We randomly sample 300 examples from the test sets of DailyDialog and ConvAI2 respectively, and recruit 6 well-educated native speakers to do qualitative analysis on the responses generated by our model and all competitive baselines, which are randomly shuffled to hide identification. The annotators judge the quality of the responses from four aspects: (1) Fluency: whether the response is fluent without any grammatical errors; (2) Relevance: whether the response is coherent with the context; (3) Informativeness: whether the response contains informative content; (4) Engagement: how much does the annotator like the response.
answer_4.guideline: Annotators assign scores from {0,1,2} representing 'bad', 'fair', 'good' for Fluency, Relevance, Informativeness, and Engagement.
